sections.body_md:
The textbook sum \(K_p e + K_i\int e + K_d \dot e\) is not what a computer should run. A pure derivative amplifies the measurement noise, and a step in the reference becomes a spike if the derivative looks at the error. The integral and the derivative also have to become updates that use samples, and a one-sample delay is part of the loop whether or not the algebra mentions it.

The practical repair is small. Filter the derivative. Let the proportional and derivative terms look at a weighted reference, often with no derivative on the reference at all. Then replace \(s\) by a discrete map and check that stable continuous poles stay inside the unit circle.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The filtered derivative is \(K_d s/(\tau_f s + 1)\) with \(\tau_f = \tau_d/N\). The filter pole sits at \(-N/\tau_d\). Setpoint weights \(b\) and \(c\) form the proportional input \(b r - y\) and the derivative input \(c r - y\). The choice \(c = 0\) keeps a reference step out of the derivative. These weights do not change the loop gain, which is still measured from \(y\).

Forward Euler uses \(z = 1 + sT\). Backward Euler uses \(z = 1/(1 - sT)\). Tustin uses \(s = (2/T)(z-1)/(z+1)\). The integral update with backward Euler adds \(K_i T\) times the current error at every sample.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(\tau_d = 0.25\) s and \(N = 5\). The filter time constant is \(0.25/5 = 0.05\) s, and the filter pole is at \(-20\) rad/s. A sample period of \(0.1\) s is a bit coarse next to that pole. Forward Euler would send a continuous pole at \(-8\) to \(z = 1 + (-8)(0.1) = 0.2\), still inside the unit circle. The same map applied to a pole at \(-50\), as in a later numerical case with a shorter period, can leave the disk. The filter corner and the sample period have to be chosen together.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Forward Euler is the easy formula and the one that can turn a stable fast pole into an unstable discrete pole. Backward Euler and Tustin do not. The factor in the integrator is \(K_i T\), not \(K_i/T\). Setpoint weighting changes the zeros from reference to output and does not retune the loop gain. And a derivative filter is not a license to sample slowly: one sample of delay is still \(\omega T\) radians of phase at the crossover.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A computational delay is a time delay in the loop, with the phase lag that delay always adds. Integral action in state feedback meets the same windup problem once the command saturates. Model-predictive controllers take the saturation into the optimization instead of repairing it afterward.
